newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mixed, but PGMs jump.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mixed, but PGMs jump.

text.p: NYMEX platinum group metals futures (PGMs) ended sharply higher Wednesday, helped by further news of a threatened strike at Russia's Norilsk mine from March 15, but COMEX gold and silver futures ended lower.
"As news of delayed Russian PGM exports continues to roil the market platinum could continue to rise though there is some resistance above $385," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
NYMEX April platinum ended up $4.90 an ounce at $386.70, after seeing a 12-week high at $388.00 intraday. Total estimated platinum volume was 8,686 contracts.
The April NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread soared further to end at $30.30 an ounce, up from $25.70 Tuesday, and only $3.20 at the start of 1997.
NYMEX June palladium closed at a new contract high at $150.25, up $6.00 for the day.

Earlier in the physical market, spot palladium in London fixed at $150.00 an ounce, its highest level since August 22, 1995, and the differential between palladium sponge and palladium plate widened to $6-8 an ounce from $5-6 an ounce, US refiners said.

Workers at Russia's Norilsk mine are threatening a strike from March 15 to force payment of wage arrears. Norilsk is a major producer of nickel, cobalt, platinum and palladium and Russian accounts for about 60 pct of world palladium supplies.
The market is also concerned about the breakdown of the Russian/Japanese supply contract talks which occurred in December 1996.

Russian exports of platinum group metals are expected to be much lower in 1997 than in 1996 and no palladium will be exported to Japan in March, a spokesman for Russia's platinum group metals export agency, Almaz, said Monday.

However, despite some early gains, COMEX gold and silver futures ended lower, after a sharp rise in US treasury bond yields, following a warning by Federal Reserve chairman Greenspan that interest rates may have to be raised pre-emptively to combat US inflation.
COMEX April gold closed down 10 cents at $356.20 an ounce, after first seeing a 20-day intraday high at $358.70, though resistance is still seen around $360.00, traders said.
Spot gold bullion ended quoted $354.00/50, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $354.75 and the New York close Tuesday at $354.00/50.

"Prices are poised to make a run at $360 over the next few days," Kempf said. "Physical demand for gold is quite strong in the Far East, Middle East and North America and gold stocks are extremely low in COMEX approved warehouses, totalling only 585,384 ounces Tuesday."
World gold demand slipped 3.7 percent to 2,624 tonnes in 1996 from the record high 2,726 tonnes in 1995, according to the World Gold Council's latest quarterly demand survey published Wednesday.
But developing market gold demand in Asia, the Middle East and Latin America edged up one percent to a record 1,825 tonnes in 1996, the Council said.
US gold demand was up six percent to a record 345.3 tonnes last year.ose to a record 1,824.8 tonnes
But investment demand for gold in developed countries fell 57 percent to 88 tonnes, a six year low, with demand weakest in Japan and Europe, the Council said.
Investment demand is the key factor in setting gold prices in the short term, analysts said.
After a year long decline from five year highs at $417 an ounce, gold prices saw three year lows at $336 in January.
COMEX May silver ended down 2.9 cents at $5.248, but not before spiking up to a six month intraday high at $5.390.

Silver prices could rise as high at $6.00 an ounce by late 1997 as the ongoing deficit between supply and demand draws down silver inventories to critically low levels, New York based industry consultants CPM Group said Tuesday;
--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641
